title: Choosing What to Be Known For: A Framework for Selecting an Institutional Signature Research Program
content: Institutions that sustain a research enterprise must periodically decide what they intend to be known for. Designating a signature research program commits recruitment, space, capital, and reputation to a single line of inquiry and, unavoidably, commits the institution to declining others. In practice, the decision is frequently made by inventory: the department producing the most publications, funding, or faculty appointments is designated the institutional strength. This article develops a structured framework for the decision, drawing on the research prioritization literature, the multi-criteria decision analysis literature, the scientometric literature on research group size and funding returns, and the literature on responsible use of research metrics. The framework comprises two threshold gates applied before any scoring, mission alignment and critical mass; six weighted domains assessed on an anchored five-point scale; two procedural disciplines, weights fixed before candidates are scored and a non-compensatory floor below which no candidate advances; and a requirement that measures of success and conditions for withdrawal be declared at the moment of designation. The framework is offered as a decision aid rather than a decision rule. It has not been prospectively evaluated, and its central claim is procedural: that the sequence in which an institution makes this decision determines the quality of the decision more reliably than the sophistication of the model it uses to make it.
